meta.title: Who really said "I have never thrown an illegal pitch. The trouble is some of my pitches were never seen by this generation until I came along"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Satchel Paige said it to the Miami Herald in March 1958, defending his hesitation pitch. He credited the pitch itself to Rube Waddell.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I have never thrown an illegal pitch. The trouble is some of my pitches were never seen by this generation until I came along'?
meta.ogDescription: Paige said it to the Miami Herald in March 1958 — and in the same breath gave the pitch away to Rube Waddell.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1906–1982 · Negro leagues and Major League pitcher
answer.sourceLine: Paige said it to the Miami Herald’s Eddie Storin for a profile published on 5 March 1958. Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes the passage; apart from a comma before “until,” it is the sentence above word for word. A United Press International story five months later carried it in exactly this form.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Psychiatrist Satch Set for Season” by Eddie Storin
Accusations that his “hesitation pitch” broke the rules

source.excerpt: “I have never thrown an illegal pitch,” he straight-faced. “The trouble is some of my pitches were never seen by this generation, until I came along. But you know a fella named (Rube) Waddell used that hesitation pitch of mine back in the 1890’s.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ gives the earliest citation as Eddie Storin, “Psychiatrist Satch Set for Season,” The Miami Herald, 5 March 1958, page 5D, column 6.

The same page records a United Press International story of 3 August 1958 printing the remark as “I’ve never thrown an illegal pitch. The trouble is some of my pitches were never seen by this generation until I came along” — the popular wording, comma and all removed, within the same year.

Quote Investigator’s conclusion: “Satchel Paige deserves credit for the remark he made by 1958. The phrasing presented in newspaper accounts has been variable, and Satchel Paige probably delivered the line more than once.”
Wikiquote ↗ carries a different wording of the same joke and cites The New York Times of 9 June 1982 — the day after Paige died. It is a real variant, but it is not this sentence.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. The only difference from the wording that circulates is the comma before “until.” The dating of Rube Waddell to “the 1890’s” is Paige’s own; we have not checked it.
source.rightsNote: First published in The Miami Herald on 5 March 1958. The United States public domain currently reaches published works from before 1931, so a 1958 newspaper is in copyright.

author.name: Satchel Paige
author.heading: About Satchel Paige
author.metaLine: 1906–1982 · Negro leagues and Major League pitcher
author.bio: Leroy Robert “Satchel” Paige began pitching in the Negro leagues with the Birmingham Black Barons in 1927 and did not reach the Major Leagues until 9 July 1948, when he debuted for the Cleveland Indians at 42. That season he became the first player who had played in the Negro leagues to pitch in a World Series. He threw his last Major League game for the Kansas City Athletics in September 1965, two weeks shy of 60, and in 1971 became the first player elected by the Hall of Fame’s Negro League Committee.

misattribution.heading: Often misquoted
misattribution.intro: The line is Paige’s and nobody disputes it. What varies — a lot — is the wording, because he told it repeatedly and reporters wrote down what they heard.

items.why: Quote Investigator’s earliest citation, and the closest documented match to the wording that circulates. Quote Investigator ↗

items.who: “I ain’t never throwed an illegal pitch”
items.why: A Rochester, New York paper printed it this way in December 1964, and a Texas paper credited Catholic Digest for a similar version in March 1965. Both render Paige in a dialect the 1958 Herald transcription does not use.

items.who: “once in a while I toss one that ain’t never been seen by this generation”
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ cites this form to The New York Times of 9 June 1982. A genuine variant from his obituary coverage — but twenty-four years later than the sentence above, and not the one people search for.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that “Satchel Paige deserves credit for the remark he made by 1958,” while warning that newspaper phrasings vary because he delivered the line more than once.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke is a defence. Paige threw a “hesitation pitch” — a stutter in the delivery that broke a batter’s timing — and it was treated as cheating. A 1964 Rochester account, quoted by Quote Investigator, says it had been banned by then American League president Will Harridge as “deceitful.”

So the line does two things at once. It denies the charge, and it explains the charge away: what looks illegal is only unfamiliar. And then, having claimed the pitch, Paige immediately gave it back — a fella named Waddell had it first.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology is short and tight: The Miami Herald (5 March 1958), United Press International (3 August 1958), the Rochester Democrat and Chronicle (5 December 1964) and the Tyler Morning Telegraph crediting Catholic Digest (10 March 1965).

Paige was pitching in the Major Leagues again in 1958, ten years after his debut season with Cleveland, and the question of his age followed him everywhere. “Never seen by this generation” is a joke about the pitch and a joke about the pitcher in the same breath.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator transcribes "I have never thrown an illegal pitch... The trouble is some of my pitches were never seen by this generation, until I came along" from The Miami Herald of 5 March 1958, p. 5D col. 6, and concludes Paige deserves credit for the remark he made by 1958.

Quote Investigator records a UPI story of 3 August 1958 printing the remark in the popular wording, and 1964 and 1965 dialect variants; it also quotes the 1964 Rochester statement that the hesitation pitch was banned by AL president Will Harridge as "deceitful".
Wikiquote carries a different wording of the same joke cited to The New York Times, June 9, 1982.
